value.overview: The Sepia-capped Flycatcher (Leptopogon amaurocephalus) is a small, quietly active tyrant flycatcher of tropical forests. It is usually found in shaded vegetation from the understory to the lower middle levels of the forest, where it makes short flights to capture insects and sometimes takes small fruits. Its broad distribution extends from Mexico through Central America and across much of northern and eastern South America. In Costa Rica, it is a resident species associated mainly with forested lowlands and foothills.
value.classification: The species belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, and the genus Leptopogon. Several geographic subspecies are recognized across its extensive range.
value.identification: This small flycatcher has olive-green upperparts, a distinctly sepia-brown crown, and a grayish face with a pale throat. The underparts are generally pale gray to yellowish, becoming more yellow toward the belly, and the wings show contrasting pale edging or wingbars. It has a short, fairly broad bill and a compact shape. In Costa Rica, careful attention to the brown crown, subdued coloration, and forest-understory habits helps separate it from other small Leptopogon flycatchers.
value.rangeHabitat: The Sepia-capped Flycatcher occurs from southern Mexico through much of Central America and across large parts of northern, western, and eastern South America. In Costa Rica, the northern Central American subspecies range reaches the central part of the country, with the species also occurring along the Pacific slope from central Costa Rica southward toward Panama. It uses lowland evergreen forest, mature secondary forest, forest edges, gallery woodland, and some plantations, generally from sea level into the foothills and lower subtropical elevations.
value.migrationStatus: It is generally considered a year-round resident rather than a long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, it is present as a resident in suitable forest habitat; major seasonal movements have not been reliably documented, although local or elevational movements may occur.
value.breeding: Detailed information on breeding is limited across much of the species' range. The breeding season is geographically variable and is not well defined for Costa Rica. Records from Mexico indicate breeding activity at least during April and May, but this should not be assumed to represent the full Costa Rican season. The species is believed to breed within its Costa Rican range, but reliable published details on nest placement, clutch size, incubation, and parental care remain sparse.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of insects and other small arthropods, with fruits also taken. It usually forages alone or in pairs in shaded vegetation from the understory to the lower middle levels of the forest. Typical feeding involves short sallies from a perch to hover-glean prey from leaves or snatch insects and fruit. It may occasionally capture flying insects and can participate in mixed-species feeding flocks.
value.behavior: This is a relatively unobtrusive forest flycatcher that often remains inside dense foliage rather than using exposed perches. Its movements are usually brief and deliberate, making it easier to detect by its calls than by prolonged views. Individuals commonly forage singly or in pairs, but they may join mixed-species flocks while feeding. As with many small tropical flycatchers, activity is concentrated in shaded woodland with a layered understory and abundant foliage.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend has not been quantified in detail, but the species is widespread and is not currently considered globally threatened.
